intro: A singing line moves inside rapidly repeated piano sonorities: keep the water’s motion separate from Ondine’s voice. This assembled Gaspard changes pianist: Andriy Makarevych plays Ondine and Scarbo; OE1FEU plays Le Gibet.
question: How does one piano distinguish a sustained voice from continuously moving water?

sections.label: Song and repeated sonorities
sections.mNote: melody distinguished from the rapid background

sections.label: The sustained crest
sections.mNote: register and weight enlarge the piano texture

sections.label: Retreat from the crest
sections.mNote: quieter figuration and more exposed phrases

sections.label: Final outburst and disappearance
sections.mNote: rapid figuration subsides into the home key

cues.title: Two speeds at once
cues.text: The opening separates rapid repeated sonorities from a much slower melodic line. Listen through the moving surface for the notes that belong to the song; a busy accompaniment does not make the melody fast.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 3: Lent, repeated right-hand sonorities and the lower melodic line marked très doux et très expressif. The report places the opening in a low relative-level range; no individual note onset is asserted.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Follow the middle register
cues.text: Across this opening span, do not assume that the highest note is the melody. Ravel places the singing voice below the repeated treble sounds, making balance between registers part of the musical argument.
cues.evidence: The opening score distinguishes the treble figuration from the slower melody below it. This is a passage-wide listening task, not a claim that a voice enters at 0:35.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A rise and withdrawal
cues.text: The early phrase swells, then gives back much of its weight. Keep following the melodic contour as the background changes; the withdrawal is not the end of Ondine’s song.
cues.evidence: The report rises from −19.9 dB at 1:00 to −14.4 at 1:10, then falls to −24.1 at 1:20. These are relative levels within this recording, not score dynamics.

cues.title: An invitation under water
cues.text: In Aloysius Bertrand’s prose poem, Ondine asks the narrator to accept her ring and become king of the lakes. He replies that he loves a mortal woman. Ravel prints the poem before the music rather than adding a singer.
cues.evidence: Bertrand’s poem, reproduced before Ondine in the Durand score; French text: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Ondine

cues.title: Waves gather weight
cues.text: In this stretch the piano grows again towards a substantial swell. Listen for the longer rise and retreat around the small ripples: Ravel organises the water figures into phrases, not a uniform wash of notes.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −21.9 dB at 2:05 to −11.9 at 2:25, then falls to −27.8 at 2:35. A measured boundary at 2:06 anchors the beginning of this broad listening region.

cues.title: A poem on the page
cues.text: Bertrand died in 1841; his collection appeared posthumously in 1842. Ravel’s score calls its movements “three poems for piano”: literary images supply the subject, but instrumental layers carry the narrative.
cues.evidence: The work’s subtitle and printed poems are in the Durand edition. Publication history and Ravel’s reading are discussed by Gerald Larner: https://geraldlarner.com/work/ravel-gaspard-de-la-nuit-1908

cues.title: Prepare for the crest
cues.text: The middle span builds a longer accumulation than the early swells. Keep a melodic thread in view as the piano spreads across registers; the broad phrase must survive the increased weight of its decoration.
cues.evidence: Durand pp. 9–11 enlarge the figuration and chordal writing. The report has a strong change at 3:36, followed by sustained higher relative level through 4:20; the score is not aligned bar by bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The largest broad swell
cues.text: Here the sustained build reaches the recording’s broadest crest. Compare it with the earlier, shorter surges: much of the force comes from keeping the phrase under pressure before allowing it to recede.
cues.evidence: The five highest five-second windows are 3:55 and 4:05–4:20, with the maximum at 4:10. The claim is about this file’s relative-level contour.

cues.title: Weight falls away
cues.text: After the crest, the texture loses weight without immediately losing motion. Listen for the difference between fewer or softer attacks and the end of a phrase; the piano can retreat while its figures continue.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −8.4 dB at 4:20 to −25.4 at 4:40; changes at 4:34 and 4:46 mark the retreat. Onsets continue through the lower-level stretch.

cues.title: Viñes introduces the triptych
cues.text: Ricardo Viñes gave the first performance of Gaspard in Paris on 9 January 1909. Ravel and Viñes had known one another as young piano students; Viñes also introduced Jeux d’eau and Miroirs.
cues.evidence: Premiere date and pianist: https://imslp.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(Ravel%2C_Maurice). Their friendship and literary interests: https://geraldlarner.com/work/ravel-gaspard-de-la-nuit-1908. Earlier premieres are documented in the site’s Ravel biography.

cues.title: The background stops flowing
cues.text: Near the end, Ravel exposes a very slow, speech-like line without the continuous water figures. This recitative makes the coming rush of notes a change of texture, not merely another increase in speed.
cues.evidence: Durand p. 13 ends with a Très lent unaccompanied line. The report’s 5:42 boundary leads into sparse, low-level windows at 5:45–6:05, supporting this approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After the last rush
cues.text: The final rush gives way to lighter arpeggios and a return towards C♯ major. Follow the remaining resonance rather than expecting a heavy closing chord: the written ending lets motion diminish before the sound disappears.
cues.evidence: Durand p. 14: Rapide et brillant, then retenez peu à peu, ppp and au mouvement du début. The report shows a late surge at 6:10–6:15, C♯-major-compatible estimates at 6:25–6:35 and a sharp decline after 6:35. Exact attacks are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The figuration carries the expansion
transitions.how: Ravel develops the contrast already established between a slower song and faster background figures. Arpeggios spread through a wider register while sustained tones continue to connect the phrases. The join is not a new instrument or a full stop: changing chord colour and the reach of the keyboard texture make the next rise feel larger.
transitions.evidence: Durand pp. 6–8 supply the expanding figuration. A 2:06 measured boundary and the 2:10–2:25 rise anchor a broad region only; this is not a claim for a specific thematic entry.

transitions.title: Small figures acquire chordal weight
transitions.how: The piano’s quick figures continue, but wider spacing and more substantial chordal writing enlarge the slower line. Ravel can increase the weight of a phrase without replacing its basic opposition of song and water. The accumulation carries across the section boundary instead of waiting for a separating cadence.
transitions.evidence: Durand pp. 9–11 show the enlarged writing; the report’s 3:36 change precedes the sustained higher-level region and crest at 3:55–4:20.

transitions.title: The waves release their weight
transitions.how: The extended crest gives way to lighter piano figuration and more exposed melodic fragments. The same instrument now separates attack from resonance more clearly. Withdrawal, rather than a new theme announced at full strength, joins the large central wave to the remaining phrases.
transitions.evidence: A measured change at 4:34 follows the decline from 4:20; the 4:35–4:45 windows are much lower in relative level. The score’s post-climactic thinning supplies the textural description, without identifying a chord at 4:34.

transitions.title: Remove the water, expose the voice
transitions.how: The continuous figuration is withdrawn, leaving a single, very slow line. Ravel writes Très lent: the contrast depends on the absence of the surrounding notes as much as on the pace. A melody formerly embedded in a layered keyboard texture can now sound like an unaccompanied utterance.
transitions.evidence: Durand p. 13, final system. The 5:42 measured change and sparse 5:45–6:05 windows support a passage-level estimate, not the exact first recitative note.

transitions.title: A rapid answer breaks the stillness
transitions.how: The isolated line gives way to a two-handed rush marked Rapide et brillant. Ravel then reduces the force and restores the opening tempo, with arpeggios settling towards C♯ major. The closing gesture answers the recitative by changing register, density and pace together, before drawing the motion back into quiet resonance.
transitions.evidence: Durand p. 14. Relative level jumps from −43.6 dB at 6:05 to −11.8 at 6:10; boundaries at 6:10 and 6:20 locate the outburst and retreat. The score supplies the markings and final tonality.

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
